A cap tells the platform when a buyer has had enough: a number of calls per day, per hour or at the same time. Caps keep buyers happy, but caps that are too tight, or that all run out together, leave good calls with no destination.
Daily or monthly caps limit total volume.
Hourly caps spread a buyer’s calls across the day.
Concurrency caps limit how many live calls a buyer takes at once, usually matching their free agents.
If every buyer is full by midday, the afternoon’s calls fail. Combine buyers with different hours and different caps, so there is always somewhere for a call to go.

When a buyer is full or misses the ring, the next eligible buyer should ring immediately. Failover turns a capped buyer from a lost call into, at worst, a slightly cheaper one.

A form that says “call me tomorrow morning” sounds clear until the lead is three time zones away. Call at 9am office time and you might wake them at 6.

A callback sequence usually has several steps: a call, a text if it is missed, another call later in the day, a last try the next morning. Space them so each lands at a sensible local hour, and stop the sequence the moment the lead answers or converts.

Retries spread through the day, never back to back.
Calling hours, holidays and contact limits vary by state. Measure every window in the lead’s own time zone, and let a step wait rather than fire outside it.

When a call could go to any of several people, the question is how to ask them. Ring them all and take whoever answers first, or try them in an order you chose?

Ringing everyone at once gets a caller to a person fastest. The caller hears fewer rings, and whoever is free picks up. It suits teams where anyone can handle any caller, such as a sales floor or agents covering one office.
The cost is fairness and focus. The same fast responder can win most calls, and people in the middle of something are interrupted by calls they will not take.

Dialing in order keeps a preference. Your first choice always gets first refusal, and the next person rings only if they do not answer. It suits partners with different priorities or skills, at the price of a longer wait when the early choices are busy.

A caller rings on Monday, hangs up, and rings again on Tuesday. Is that one lead or two? In pay-per-call the answer decides who gets paid, so it is worth settling in writing before the first call arrives.

A duplicate window is the stretch of time in which a second call from the same number counts as a repeat rather than a new lead. Inside the window the repeat is not paid for again; outside it, the caller is treated as new.

Length follows the sales cycle. Quick purchases suit short windows; considered ones, where people call back to compare quotes, suit longer ones. The window also needs a scope, because a repeat to the same buyer is a different question from a repeat to the same offer.
Same buyer, short window: a buyer never pays twice for someone calling back.
Same offer, longer window: a source is not paid twice for one shopper.
Whole account: the strictest view, useful in small verticals.

Blocked and anonymous caller IDs cannot be matched, so decide up front whether they always count as new or always go to review. Shared office lines and family phones can also look like repeats; a shorter window keeps them from being shut out unfairly.
Write the window, its scope and the anonymous-caller rule into every buyer and source agreement. Most duplicate disputes are really arguments about a rule nobody wrote down.

A Rule of Thumb for Sizing
Signs the Pool Is Too Tight

Dynamic number insertion works by lending each website visitor their own tracking number for a while. When they call, the number points back to their visit, and so to the ad, keyword and tokens behind it. The lending only works if there are enough numbers to go around.

Each number stays with a visitor for as long as they might plausibly call: while they browse, and for a little while after. If more people are on the site at once than there are numbers in the pool, two visitors end up holding the same one, and a call to it can no longer be traced to a single visit.

Size for your busiest hour, not your average one. Estimate how many visitors are on the pages that show a number at the same moment, and give each of them a number for the length of a typical visit, with some headroom on top.

Calling leads and running outbound campaigns carries legal exposure, and most of it traces back to a handful of familiar gaps: no proof of consent, numbers that should never have been dialed, and calls placed at the wrong hour.
Record consent when the lead submits, including the exact wording they agreed to.
Keep a verifiable record with each lead: the time, the page and the consent text.

Check each number at the moment it is about to be dialed, not in a monthly batch. Use national and internal do-not-call lists, plus suppression lists for numbers that must not be contacted for a particular buyer, offer or campaign.
A blacklist blocks a number across your whole account; a suppression list blocks it only where you attach it. Most programs need both.

Limit who can view phone numbers and other personal fields.
Strip personal details from call transcriptions.
Clear or hash personal data once records pass your retention period.
If a complaint arrives, you will need to show when consent was given, which checks ran and why the call was allowed. Store that record alongside the call, where anyone can find it quickly.

Every pay-per-call deal rests on one definition: when does a call count? Settle it clearly and both sides trust the numbers. Leave it vague and every invoice turns into a negotiation.
Duration: the call counts once it passes a set number of seconds.
Press 1 to accept: the buyer confirms they want the call, and the timer starts from that moment.
Postback: the buyer reports a conversion from their own system, such as a sale or a booked appointment.

A duration rule is simple and quick to settle, but it rewards long calls rather than good ones. Press 1 to accept protects buyers from paying for calls that ring into a busy floor or an IVR they never wanted. A postback pays on real outcomes, but only as well as the buyer reports them.

Match the rule to the vertical. Fast, high-volume verticals often settle on duration. Higher-value calls, where a buyer may screen several callers before one buys, lean toward press 1 or a postback. Whichever you pick, write the threshold, the moment the timer starts and the payout type into the agreement.
Changing the rule mid-campaign breaks every before-and-after comparison. If it has to change, start a new offer rather than editing the old one.
